d.title: There is no term for truth in the objective
d.caption: Next-token prediction maximises the probability of a **plausible continuation** given the prefix, and there is no term in that objective for truth and no internal signal distinguishing a remembered fact from a well-shaped guess. **So hallucination is the default rather than a fault** — 1.1 showed the same structure from the sampling side: the model always produces *something*, and nothing in the mechanism can return nothing. The consequence runs through the whole module: **abstention is a capability you have to add.**

d.title: Four terms, and the distinction that decides what you can measure
d.caption: **Faithfulness is answerable and factuality is not** — at least not cheaply. Faithfulness asks whether the answer is supported by **the context you supplied**, which is sitting right there in the request. Factuality asks whether it matches the real world, which needs an external source of truth. That is why every measurable metric in this module is a faithfulness metric, and why **a perfectly faithful answer can still be false** if the context was.

d.title: Six causes, and the fix for each lives in a different place
d.caption: **A retrieval miss is the most common cause**, which means the first fix for hallucination is usually not a prompt change at all — it is hybrid search and a reranker. Two of the six are prompt-level and free: an ungrounded prompt and a missing abstention path. The rest are an indexing problem, a context-length problem, and a conflict between what the model was told and what it already believes.

d.title: If the instruction set contains no acceptable 'I don't know', the model guesses
d.caption: This follows directly from 11.1's mechanism. The objective rewards a plausible continuation, and **if no acceptable abstention exists in the instruction set, the most plausible continuation is a guess.** Adding an explicit out removes a large fraction of RAG hallucinations, because the model is no longer choosing between inventing and disobeying. And it pairs with an operational metric: 11.6 tracks abstention rate **in both directions** — too low means overconfident, too high means retrieval is weak.

d.title: It did not invent a number — it extended a real policy to an uncovered case
d.caption: Retrieval returned a **generic** refund chunk; the specific *opened software* clause was in a chunk that was not retrieved. Notice what the model did **not** do: it did not invent a figure from nothing. **It took a real policy from a real retrieved chunk and extended it to a case the chunk did not cover** — which is why the output is so convincing and why a citation check passes it. The fix has two halves: better chunking plus a reranker so the clause is retrievable, and an instruction to abstain when the documents do not cover the case.

nodes.label: And a citation check passes it

d.title: The fake citation is our instruction, not the model's failing
d.caption: The root cause is a **combination**: a closed-book factual question means the model has no context to ground in, and a *cite your sources* instruction means the output must contain something citation-shaped. **Asking for citations from a model with no retrieval is asking it to invent them** — this is 11.1's leading-prompt trigger, and the prompt created it. The fix is structural rather than persuasive: only allow citations that map to retrieved documents, and post-validate every id against the set that was actually supplied.

d.title: Entailment separates supported from unsupported by two orders of magnitude
d.caption: Four sentences, three supported and one inventing a $50,000 termination penalty, gives faithfulness of 1 − 1/4 = **0.75**. Entailment is a **three-way** output so a decision rule is needed — and the reason any of the three rules works is the separation: **supported claims score 0.9888 to 0.9931 and unsupported ones 0.0009 to 0.0221.** Two orders of magnitude apart, which is what makes the threshold choice uncritical rather than delicate.

d.title: Cosine similarity's best threshold is 86%, and its top-scoring claim is the hallucination
d.caption: Cosine between context and claim is the obvious cheap substitute, and it fails in the worst possible way. **The single highest-scoring claim is the hallucination**: *"You have 30 days to return opened software"* scores **0.8108** against the true *"14 days"* — because it is lexically almost identical and semantically opposite. The best achievable accuracy over any threshold is **86% against a 57% majority baseline**, and the errors are concentrated exactly where it matters.

d.title: Neither signal belongs in the request path
d.caption: `roberta-large-mnli` is 355M parameters and runs **a separate forward pass over the whole context per claim**, so cost scales with claims × context length: **739 ms per claim, 2,957 ms for a four-claim answer** on CPU. And 10.11 measured an LLM judge at 107% of the generation it scores. So the conclusion is not *use a judge instead* — it is that **neither belongs in the request path at these latencies**, and a blocking faithfulness gate is an offline or sampled check wearing a synchronous costume.

d.title: Four of six causes, in seven lines of prompt, at zero cost
d.caption: Each line targets a specific cause from 11.2. *"ONLY the provided context"* fixes the ungrounded prompt; rule 1 supplies the abstention path; rule 2 addresses the parametric conflict. **That is four of the six causes addressed in seven lines, at zero latency and zero marginal cost** — the remaining two are a retrieval miss and a stale index, which no prompt can reach. Note the exact-wording requirement in rule 1: **specifying the precise abstention string is what makes abstention measurable**, because 11.6 counts it with a string match.

d.title: A citation that resolves is not a citation that supports
d.caption: 11.3 measured this directly: **an answer citing a real, retrieved chunk while claiming the opposite of what the chunk says passes the subset check cleanly.** So citation accuracy needs two checks — validate the cited ids, which is free and structural, **and** run entailment, which is not. One practical trap from the same measurement: a validator written for opaque ids like `c12` finds **zero citations** in `[refund-policy]`, so it reports perfect compliance on an answer it never parsed.

d.title: Three decoding choices for faithfulness rather than creativity
d.caption: These are the cheapest interventions in the layer and the easiest to forget, because they are parameters rather than prose. **Capping `max_tokens` is the direct structural bound on confabulation** — the model cannot run past the supported content if it cannot keep generating. And structured output with a **nullable** field is an abstention path expressed in a schema, which is 1.8's strict-mode rule put to a safety use.

d.title: Verify-then-serve is not deployable as written
d.caption: 11.4 timed the NLI model at 739 ms per claim, so a four-claim answer is **2,957 ms against a 3,134 ms request — a 94% latency overhead**. The honest options are a small NLI model, a GPU, or gating only the sampled share. The **0.9 threshold also deserves a look**: with a four-sentence answer, claims are scored in quarters — 0.75 or 1.0, nothing between — so a 0.9 threshold is really "all four claims must pass", and saying that is clearer than quoting a decimal.

d.title: Six metrics, and the one that has to be read in both directions
d.caption: Five of these have a direction: higher faithfulness is better, lower hallucination rate is better. **Abstention rate does not** — too low means the model is overconfident and too high means retrieval is weak, so the number is uninterpretable without context recall beside it. And citation accuracy is the one that needs two mechanisms rather than one: **validate the ids and run entailment**, because 11.5 showed the first alone passes a contradiction.

d.title: The same system, the same metric, opposite conclusions
d.caption: **An abstention makes no claims, and the fraction of an empty set is 1.0 by construction** — so every refusal is a perfect faithfulness score. The consequence is worse than a bias: as context recall degrades from 0.93 to 0.20, **overall faithfulness barely moves**, because the system increasingly abstains and each abstention scores 1.0. Computed over **answered requests only**, the same system falls 0.920 to 0.750 monotonically. Same data, same metric name, opposite reading — and the first version would never have paged anyone.

d.title: The golden set needs cases whose right answer is an abstention
d.caption: **A golden case whose correct answer is an abstention is the only way to test the abstention path**, and without such cases a system that never abstains scores perfectly. Run the set on every prompt change *and* every model change, because both can silently regress grounding — 12.4 is about the version that changes without you. And size it honestly: 9.16's arithmetic applies unchanged, so **a ten-case set measuring a 0.20 hallucination rate carries ±24.8 points**, which is not a measurement.
